```{r}
#| label: setup-plots
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(see)
report_theme <- function() {
  see::theme_modern(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#E6EBEF", linewidth = 0.3),
          axis.title = element_text(colour = "#294C60"),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = "#495865"),
          plot.margin = margin(10, 14, 8, 10))
}
dat <- read.csv("The_Significant_Five_dataset.csv",
                colClasses = c(studentID = "character"))
stopifnot(nrow(dat) == 92, !anyNA(dat))

d <- dat
n <- nrow(d)

```

# Summary Statistics

## Numerical Variables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-numeric
numeric_vars <- c("budget_cad", "judgment_worry", "general_embarrassment",
                  "communication_discomfort", "max_wtp_cad")
numeric_labels <- c("Budget", "Judgment worry", "General embarrassment",
                    "Communication discomfort", "Maximum WTP")
summary_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = numeric_labels,
  Median = sapply(d[numeric_vars], median),
  Mean = sapply(d[numeric_vars], mean),
  SD = sapply(d[numeric_vars], sd),
  IQR = sapply(d[numeric_vars], IQR),
  Range = sapply(d[numeric_vars], function(x) paste(range(x), collapse = "-")),
  n = n, row.names = NULL)
for (j in 2:5) {
  summary_table[[j]] <- sprintf("%.2f", summary_table[[j]])
  summary_table[[j]][c(1, 5)] <- paste0("$", summary_table[[j]][c(1, 5)])
}
summary_table$Range[c(1, 5)] <- sapply(d[c("budget_cad", "max_wtp_cad")],
  function(x) paste0("$", min(x), "-$", max(x)))
knitr::kable(summary_table, align = "lrrrrlr",
  caption = "Numerical summaries (n = 92). SD: standard deviation; IQR: interquartile range.")
```

## Categorical Variables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-categorical
qual_vars <- c("student_status", "embarrassed_easily", "self_conscious",
               "pay5_lateness", "buy20_shirt")
qual_labels <- c("Student status", "Easily embarrassed", "Self-conscious after mistakes",
                 "Pay $5 to avoid explaining lateness", "Buy $20 replacement shirt")
freq_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(qual_vars), function(i) {
  counts <- table(d[[qual_vars[i]]])
  response <- names(counts)
  if (i > 1) response <- c("No", "Yes")[as.integer(response) + 1]
  data.frame(Variable = qual_labels[i], Response = response,
             n = as.vector(counts), Percent = round(100 * as.vector(counts) / n, 2))
}))
knitr::kable(freq_table, digits = 2,
  caption = "Categorical frequencies. No values were missing; binary items use No = 0 and Yes = 1.")
```

## Interpretation

All 92 responses were complete. Budget and maximum willingness to pay (WTP) were right-skewed: their means exceeded their medians. Median WTP was \$0, with 60 zero responses and a maximum of \$150. Most respondents reported being easily embarrassed or self-conscious. Payment willingness differed between the lateness (22.83%) and replacement-shirt (61.96%) scenarios; because both price and context differed, this comparison cannot isolate a price effect.

# Model Assumptions

Q-Q, residual-distribution, residual-versus-fitted and scale-location plots assess normality and variance homogeneity in two supplementary regressions. The primary analyses use Spearman correlation, two-proportion z-tests and Cronbach's alpha.

```{r}
#| label: setup-regression-diagnostics
#| include: false
regression_diagnostics <- function(model) {
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.3, 4.3, 2.5, 1),
                 col.main = "#294C60", col.lab = "#294C60", col.axis = "#495865",
                 mgp = c(2.6, 0.8, 0), cex = 0.85)
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  residual <- residuals(model)
  standardized <- rstandard(model)
  fitted <- fitted(model)
  qqnorm(standardized, main = "Normal Q-Q", pch = 16,
         col = "#496785", ylab = "Standardized residuals")
  qqline(standardized, col = "#D76A2B", lwd = 2)
  dens <- density(residual)
  grid <- seq(min(dens$x), max(dens$x), length.out = 300)
  normal <- dnorm(grid, mean(residual), sd(residual))
  plot(dens, main = "Residual distribution", xlab = "Residuals",
       ylim = c(0, max(dens$y, normal)), col = "#496785", lwd = 2)
  lines(grid, normal, col = "#D76A2B", lwd = 2)
  plot(fitted, residual, main = "Residuals vs fitted", pch = 16,
       col = "#496785", xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals")
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey70", lty = 2)
  lines(lowess(fitted, residual), col = "#D76A2B", lwd = 2)
  spread <- sqrt(abs(standardized))
  plot(fitted, spread, main = "Scale-location", pch = 16,
       col = "#496785", xlab = "Fitted values",
       ylab = expression(sqrt(abs("Standardized residual"))))
  lines(lowess(fitted, spread), col = "#D76A2B", lwd = 2)
}
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Model 1: Budget and Maximum Willingness to Pay

The first model examines the linear association between monthly discretionary budget and maximum willingness to pay:

$$
\text{Maximum WTP}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{Budget}_i + \varepsilon_i.
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-assumptions-budget
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for maximum WTP regressed on budget. The long upper tail and uneven residual spread raise concerns about normality and constant variance."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-pos: H
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-align: center
model1 <- lm(max_wtp_cad ~ budget_cad, data = dat)
regression_diagnostics(model1)
```

The residuals have a pronounced upper tail and uneven spread across fitted values, raising concerns about normality and constant variance. The residual-versus-fitted smooth also departs from zero. Ordinary regression inference is therefore not used for the primary budget-WTP conclusion.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Model 2: General Embarrassment and Communication Discomfort

The second model examines the linear association between general embarrassment and communication discomfort:

$$
\text{General embarrassment}_i = \alpha_0 +
\alpha_1\text{Communication discomfort}_i + \varepsilon_i.
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-assumptions-embarrassment
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for general embarrassment regressed on communication discomfort. Residuals are roughly symmetric, with a modest increase in spread at higher fitted values."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-pos: H
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-align: center
model2 <- lm(general_embarrassment ~ communication_discomfort, data = dat)
regression_diagnostics(model2)
```

Residuals are approximately symmetric, with small Q-Q departures and a modest increase in spread at higher fitted values. Normality is approximately satisfied; the slight change in spread suggests some variance heterogeneity.

# Statistical Results

## Methods

Analyses used 92 complete responses, treated as an independent random sample. Two-sided tests used a 0.05 significance level with Holm adjustment across 14 comparisons (Holm, 1979; Appendix A). Results are exploratory; 95% CIs are pointwise. Descriptive checks used `datawizard`.

## RQ1: Budget and Maximum Willingness to Pay

To address proposal RQ1, Spearman's correlation tested zero rank association between monthly discretionary budget and maximum WTP (Spearman, 1904). Ties use an approximate p-value; the CI uses 20,000 whole-respondent bootstrap resamples (Efron, 1979).

The correlation was **0.138** (95% CI **[-0.077, 0.335]**; raw p = 0.188; adjusted p = **0.376**): insufficient evidence of a monotonic association.

## RQ2: Payment Rates by Student Status

Following proposal RQ2, two-proportion z-tests assessed equal payment probabilities for Domestic and International students within each scenario, using a pooled proportion under the null and no continuity correction. The lateness comparison has only four Domestic Yes responses, limiting the normal approximation.

| Scenario | Domestic: Yes/total (%) | International: Yes/total (%) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Pay CAD 5 for lateness | 4/58 (6.9%) | 17/34 (50.0%) |
| Buy CAD 20 replacement shirt | 31/58 (53.4%) | 26/34 (76.5%) |

: Payment intentions by student status (n = 92). International students reported higher rates in both scenarios.

For lateness, the International-minus-Domestic difference was **43.1 percentage points** (95% CI **[24.5, 59.6]**; z = 4.755; raw p = 1.99e-06; adjusted p = **2.58e-05**), providing evidence of a group difference. For the shirt, it was **23.0 percentage points** (95% CI **[2.5, 39.8]**; z = 2.195; raw p = 0.028; adjusted p = **0.141**), which was not significant after adjustment. Proportion-difference CIs use the Newcombe-Wilson method (Newcombe, 1998); significance is based on Holm-adjusted p-values.

## RQ3: Internal Consistency of the Three Ratings

For proposal RQ3, raw Cronbach's alpha for the three rating items (Q5-Q7: judgment worry, general embarrassment and communication discomfort) was **0.793** (95% bootstrap CI **[0.688, 0.861]**; Cronbach, 1951). All items are positively oriented 1-10 ratings; the CI uses 20,000 whole-respondent resamples. The raw Cronbach's alpha of 0.793 suggests acceptable internal consistency among the three rating items in this sample.

## Statistical Tests

The code reproduces RQ1, RQ2 and RQ3. All 14 earlier tests remain in the Holm family; the other five WTP correlations are supplementary. Alpha is an estimation coefficient and is not added to the test family.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-tests-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
vars <- c("budget_cad", "embarrassed_easily", "self_conscious",
          "judgment_worry", "general_embarrassment",
          "communication_discomfort")
stopifnot(n == 92, !anyNA(d[c(vars, "max_wtp_cad",
                            "pay5_lateness", "buy20_shirt")]))

# Spearman tests and pointwise respondent-bootstrap intervals.
set.seed(20261019)
idx <- replicate(20000, sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE))
ci <- function(x) quantile(x[is.finite(x)], c(.025, .975), type = 7)
rho <- function(x, y) cor(x, y, method = "spearman")
spearman <- function(x, y) cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman",
                                   exact = FALSE)
correlations <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars, function(v) {
  t <- spearman(d[[v]], d$max_wtp_cad)
  draws <- apply(idx, 2, function(i) rho(d[[v]][i], d$max_wtp_cad[i]))
  limits <- ci(draws)
  data.frame(variable = v, rho = unname(t$estimate),
             low = limits[1], high = limits[2], p = t$p.value)
}))

# Descriptive scenario comparison; preserve the paired test only for Holm accounting.
tab <- table(factor(d$pay5_lateness, 0:1),
             factor(d$buy20_shirt, 0:1))
paired <- binom.test(tab[1, 2], tab[1, 2] + tab[2, 1], p = .5)


# Retain all seven supplementary tests in the original 14-test family.
pos <- d$max_wtp_cad > 0
extra_p <- c(
  spearman(d$budget_cad[pos], d$max_wtp_cad[pos])$p.value,
  spearman(d$budget_cad, as.integer(pos))$p.value)
for (v in c("pay5_lateness", "buy20_shirt", "any_positive_wtp")) {
  y <- if (v == "any_positive_wtp") as.integer(pos) else d[[v]]
  counts <- table(factor(d$student_status,
                         c("Domestic", "International")), factor(y, 0:1))
  if (v %in% c("pay5_lateness", "buy20_shirt")) {
    ni <- sum(counts[2, ]); nd <- sum(counts[1, ])
    ki <- counts[2, 2]; kd <- counts[1, 2]
    pooled <- (ki+kd)/(ni+nd)
    se <- sqrt(pooled*(1-pooled)*(1/ni+1/nd))
    z <- (ki/ni-kd/nd)/se
    extra_p <- c(extra_p, 2*pnorm(-abs(z)))
  } else {
    extra_p <- c(extra_p, fisher.test(counts)$p.value)
  }
}
for (v in c("budget_cad", "max_wtp_cad")) {
  t <- wilcox.test(d[[v]] ~ d$student_status,
                   exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE)
  extra_p <- c(extra_p, t$p.value)
}
p_all <- c(correlations$p, paired$p.value, extra_p)
stopifnot(length(p_all) == 14)
adjusted <- p.adjust(p_all, method = "holm")
correlations$holm_p <- adjusted[1:6]
# RQ1: budget-WTP association; other correlations remain supplementary.
correlations[1, ]

# RQ2: International minus Domestic risk differences and Newcombe-Wilson CIs.
wilson <- function(k, n) {
  z <- qnorm(.975); p <- k/n; den <- 1 + z^2/n
  centre <- (p + z^2/(2*n))/den
  half <- z/den * sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z^2/(4*n^2))
  c(low = max(0, centre-half), high = min(1, centre+half))
}
newcombe <- function(ki, ni, kd, nd) {
  pi <- ki/ni; pd <- kd/nd
  wi <- wilson(ki, ni); wd <- wilson(kd, nd); delta <- pi-pd
  c(low = unname(delta-sqrt((pi-wi[1])^2+(wd[2]-pd)^2)),
    high = unname(delta+sqrt((wi[2]-pi)^2+(pd-wd[1])^2)))
}
rq2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(c("pay5_lateness", "buy20_shirt")), function(j) {
  v <- c("pay5_lateness", "buy20_shirt")[j]
  tab <- table(factor(d$student_status, c("Domestic", "International")),
               factor(d[[v]], 0:1))
  nd <- sum(tab[1, ]); ni <- sum(tab[2, ])
  kd <- unname(tab[1, 2]); ki <- unname(tab[2, 2])
  limits <- newcombe(ki, ni, kd, nd)
  pooled <- (ki+kd)/(ni+nd)
  z <- (ki/ni-kd/nd)/sqrt(pooled*(1-pooled)*(1/ni+1/nd))
  # Independent check: uncorrected Pearson proportions test gives X-squared = z^2.
  check <- prop.test(c(ki, kd), c(ni, nd), correct = FALSE)
  stopifnot(abs(unname(check$statistic)-z^2) < 1e-10)
  data.frame(scenario = v, domestic_yes = kd, domestic_n = nd,
    international_yes = ki, international_n = ni,
    difference = ki/ni-kd/nd, low = limits[1], high = limits[2],
    z = unname(z), p = 2*pnorm(-abs(z)), holm_p = adjusted[9+j])
}))
rq2

# RQ3: raw Cronbach alpha and a whole-respondent bootstrap CI.
item_vars <- c("judgment_worry", "general_embarrassment",
               "communication_discomfort")
items <- as.matrix(d[item_vars])
raw_alpha <- function(x) {
  k <- ncol(x); total_variance <- var(rowSums(x))
  if (!is.finite(total_variance) || total_variance <= 0) return(NA_real_)
  k/(k-1) * (1-sum(apply(x, 2, var))/total_variance)
}
set.seed(20261025)
alpha_draws <- replicate(20000,
  raw_alpha(items[sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE), , drop = FALSE]))
stopifnot(sum(is.finite(alpha_draws)) >= .99*20000)
rq3 <- c(alpha = raw_alpha(items), ci(alpha_draws))
rq3

# Actual easystats use; base R summaries use type-7 IQRs.
datawizard::describe_distribution(d[numeric_vars],
  centrality = c("mean", "median"), iqr = FALSE)

```
